info.name: Board Game Platform — backend :3000
info.description:
The public REST surface of `backend/`, as it stands at the end of **Phase D (S17–S20)**.

## Import and run

1. Import this file **and** an environment: `Template.local.postman_environment.json` (port 3000, the normal one) or `Template.local-3999.postman_environment.json` (fallback). Then **select it in the environment dropdown, top right** — an unselected environment is the single most common reason this collection appears broken.
2. Start the API: `cd backend && npm run db:reset && npm run dev`.
3. **Run the whole collection in order** (Collection Runner), or click through the folders top to bottom. Requests capture ids into collection variables for the ones that follow, so order matters.

Every request carries assertions, so a collection run is a real smoke test: 0 failures means the surface behaves. It is *not* a replacement for `npm test` — the 708 vitest cases cover concurrency, audit rows and the leak checks that HTTP cannot express.

## ⚠ Everything 429s?

A full run is 58 requests and the global limiter allows 100 per minute per IP, so **two runs inside a minute trip it**. Wait a minute, or set `RATE_LIMIT_MAX=1000` in `backend/.env` while API testing. `/health` and `/ready` are exempt from the limiter, so they keep passing while everything else fails — which is itself the tell.

## ⚠ Everything 404s?

Then something is listening on that port and it is **not this backend**. Run the first request in folder `00 Health`: it fails with an explicit message when the responder sends `X-Powered-By` or HTML, because this API disables that header and always answers JSON. A stray `node`/Express process on :3000 will 404 every path here and look exactly like a broken collection.

On Windows: `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen` names the owner, `Stop-Process -Id <pid>` frees it. `backend/.env` sets `PORT`, and note the frontend's Vite proxy targets :3000 — so freeing 3000 is better than moving the API.

## Three things to know

**No `Authorization` header anywhere.** Identity travels in httpOnly cookies (`07` §5.3), and Postman's cookie jar holds them automatically. Nothing here needs a token pasted in.

**No `X-CSRF-Token` header either.** CSRF protection demands the double-submit token only from requests carrying an `Origin` or `Referer` — i.e. from browsers, the only clients with an ambient cookie jar to ride. Postman sends neither, so it is exempt by construction, not by a dev-only switch. If you add an `Origin` header by hand, you must also send `X-CSRF-Token` matching the `csrf` cookie, or you will get 403 `ORIGIN_MISMATCH`.

**A logged-in user masks a guest.** `authenticate` resolves the access cookie *before* the guest cookie, so with both in the jar you are always the user. Folder `06` clears the jar before the guest flow and logs back in afterwards — don't reorder those requests.

## Coverage

| Folder | Sessions | Routes |
|---|---|---|
| 00 Health | S10 | `/health`, `/ready`, both mount points |
| 01 Auth | S13–S14 | register, login, me, refresh |
| 02 Games | S17 | `/games`, `/games/:slug` |
| 03 Tables | S18 | create, mine, detail, patch |
| 04 Invites | S19 | mint, list, resolve (public), revoke |
| 05 Seats | S20 | claim, bot, release (dev-only `/_probe`) |
| 06 Guest | S16, S18 | `/auth/guest`, the table binding |
| 07 Boundary | S12 | validation, coercion, unknown keys, 404s |
| 08 Teardown | S13, S18–S19 | close table, logout |

Phase E (S21–S22) adds `/wallet`; Phase F moves live table traffic to Socket.IO, which Postman cannot exercise — `backend/scripts/dev-socket.ts` (S23) is the tool for that.

item.name: 00 Health & readiness
item.description: Two endpoints answering two different questions. Conflating them produces the classic outage: the DB hiccups, every replica reports unhealthy, and the restart storm outlasts the hiccup.

request.description: No dependency checks, deliberately: a database blip must never make the orchestrator kill a working process.

pm.variables.replaceIn('{{baseUrl}}') + ' but it is NOT this backend: it sent ' +

request.description: Throttled 5 per 15 min per email **and** per IP. Either key alone has a hole: per-IP lets one attacker spray one password across thousands of accounts; per-email lets a botnet grind one account from thousands of addresses.

A wrong password and an unknown email are deliberately indistinguishable — same code, same shape, and the timing is equalised so the response cannot be used to enumerate which addresses have accounts.

request.description:
Rotates inside the token family. Replaying an already-rotated token kills the whole family and writes an ALERT `BAD_TOKEN` event — worth trying by hand with a copy of the old cookie, though Postman's jar overwrites it for you here.

After this runs, the jar holds the *new* refresh token; the previous one is dead.

item.description: Creates two tables and captures their ids: `tableId` for everything below, `otherTableId` for the guest-binding check in folder 06.

request.description:
★ Note what did *not* happen: you are not seated. Sitting down is a separate act with its own authorization, its own race and — from S24 — its own socket event the whole table watches. A host auto-seated at seat 0 could then never choose seat 2, because one identity holds one seat per table.

`options` comes back post-parse with defaults filled in, and that is what is stored: the row records the options the game will actually be played with, so it stays replayable a year later after a default moves.

request.description: Folder 06 uses this one to prove a guest token for table A is worth nothing at table B.

★ The transport rule, and the response is defined as much by its absences as its contents (`02` §3.1). This answers *who is sitting where*. Cards, hands, turn order, legal moves and the board travel over the socket, projected once per viewer — the only path with a `projectState` boundary on it.

If a `deck` or `turn` key ever shows up here, the split has been breached and M1's leak-test suite will be guarding a door that is already open.

item.name: 04 Invites (S19)
item.description: Mints two links: `inviteCode`, which gets revoked here to prove dead links are indistinguishable, and `guestInviteCode`, which folder 06 uses to join as a guest.

request.description:
Host only. An empty body means "all defaults", which is the common case.

`joinPath` is `/t/<code>`: the server owns the link shape, so changing it later is one edit rather than a grep for string concatenation in the client.

The alphabet excludes `I L O U 0 1` — every one of those is a character that gets mistyped off a phone screen or misheard on a call, and a link that fails once is a friend who does not join.

item.name: POST /tables/:id/invites — one for the guest flow

request.description: A link with a life and a use budget of its own.

exec: pm.test('200 with both links, newest first', () => {

request.description:
★ **The point of S19.** This route takes no authentication at all, and that is the entire feature: the friend opening your link is in a private window with an empty cookie jar. If this endpoint asked who they were, journey J1→J2 would die here and a thirty-second join would become a signup funnel.

To see it properly, open a Postman console tab with cookies cleared — or just note that nothing in the request depends on the jar.

Read the payload for what it withholds: no table id, no host user id, no email, no options, no game state. A stranger deciding whether to join needs the game (as an i18n key), the host's name, and whether there is room.

exec: pm.test('★ leaks no PII, no ids, no game state', () => {

request.description: A tombstone, not a delete: the row stays, and the guests who joined through it keep pointing at it. Revoking twice is idempotent.
Compare this response with the next request's, byte for byte.

exec: // Kept for the next request to compare against.

request.description:
★ Revoked, expired, exhausted, dangling and never-existed are **one answer**, byte for byte. Any difference between them — a distinct code, an extra `details` field, even a different message — turns the one public endpoint that takes a secret into an oracle for enumerating live codes (`07` §5.2).

The reason is recorded in an `INVITE_ABUSE` audit row instead, where it is useful and invisible to whoever supplied the code. Spray a few bad codes and check `SecurityEvent` in Studio; past 30/min you also get a 429 with `retryAfterMs`, this route's own budget.

exec: pm.test('★ byte-identical to the revoked code — no enumeration oracle', () => {

item.name: 05 Seats — dev-only stand-in (S20)
item.description:
⚠ These three routes live on `/_probe` and are **deleted in S24**. Seat changes are socket traffic — if a friend at the table would watch it happen, it goes over the socket (`02` §3.1) — but S20's concurrency work lands four sessions before the gateway, and "claim it twice → 409" is worth being able to run by hand. `table:takeSeat` will call the very same `TableService.claimSeat`.

Mounted only when `NODE_ENV !== 'production'`.

**The headline check of S20 cannot be done here.** You cannot click two buttons in the same millisecond, so the concurrent claim is proven in `tests/integration/seat-claim.test.ts` — two racers, then four, each leaving exactly one occupant.

request.description: ★ The seat is in the body; the **occupant never is**. Identity comes from your cookie (and from the socket, from S24), so no payload can claim to be someone else. There is no `userId` field to send — the schema is `.strict()`, and folder 07 proves sending one is a 400.

One identity, one seat per table — enforced by `(tableId, userId)`, not by a check. `details.reason` distinguishes "you are already sitting here" (with `yourSeat`) from "that seat is taken": both are 409s, and they are different problems with different buttons to press.
`HOST_REQUIRED` for anyone else. A bot renders from `botDifficulty` plus an i18n key, so its `displayName` is null by design.

exec: pm.test('201 with a bot in seat 3', () => {

request.description: A 400, not a 409: "seat 7 is taken" would be a lie about a four-seat table.

★ While `WAITING` the row goes and the seat is free again. Once the table is `IN_PROGRESS` the behaviour deliberately flips: the row stays and `disconnectedAt` is stamped, because the seat belongs to the **match** now — it holds the player's cards, chips and reward eligibility (`04` §5.2). Vacating it would delete a hand mid-play.

That difference is asserted in `seat-claim.test.ts`; you cannot see it here until a game can start (S28–S30).

exec: pm.test('200 and seat 1 is empty again', () => {

request.description:
Run against the *second* table, because you cannot be both a player and a spectator at one table — `(tableId, userId)` is unique.

Spectators carry `seat: null`, which is exactly why any number of them coexist: that unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct on both SQLite and Postgres.

exec: pm.test('201 and the spectator is counted', () => {

item.name: 07 The boundary (S12)
item.description: `POST /_probe` exists for exactly this: one deliberately picky schema that makes each boundary guarantee visible to a client. Dev-only.

exec: pm.test('200 and the body is echoed back parsed', () => {

request.description:
★ No `z.coerce` in a body schema, ever. A string where a number belongs means the client has a bug, and silently coercing it hides that bug until it produces wrong data somewhere expensive.

★ And read the `fieldErrors` **values**: `errors.field.invalidType`, never Zod's "Expected number, received string". That English is kept in the server log, where a developer reads it, and never crosses the wire to a Persian-speaking user.

exec: pm.test('★ every field error is an i18n key, not English prose', () => {

request.description: `.strict()` everywhere. An unknown key is usually a renamed field the client did not follow, and accepting it means quietly ignoring what the caller asked for.
`express.json()`'s own parse failures are translated to 400. As opaque 500s they would read as "the server is broken" when the request was simply bad.

item.name: ★ POST /_probe/tables/:id/seats — cannot claim to be someone else

request.description: ★ Seat identity comes from the authenticated caller, never from the payload. There is no field with which to name an occupant, so this is a 400 rather than an impersonation.

exec: pm.test('400 — no such field to send', () => {

request.description: An unknown path is an `AppError` like any other: a machine `code` and an `i18nKey`, never a rendered English sentence and never an HTML error page.

S15 builds the metrics registry but exposes no HTTP route. `/metrics` and `/security-events` belong to the admin process (S49) — putting them on :3000 behind a role check is exactly the arrangement the admin-isolation rule exists to prevent.

item.name: 08 Teardown
item.description: Closes the table and ends the session. Run last — everything above needs both.

request.description: 204, and in Studio the row is `CLOSED` with `closedAt` set — **never deleted**. The event log, match results and ledger rows all reference this table, and a cascade would erase the history that pays people. Closing twice is idempotent.
No new join links for a table nobody can join.

Revokes the whole refresh-token family and clears the cookies regardless of what the server found — "log me out" has exactly one acceptable outcome from the browser's side.

This is why the refresh cookie's path is `/api/v1/auth` rather than `/api/v1/auth/refresh`: logout has to *read* it to revoke the family it belongs to.

exec: pm.test('401 — the session is gone', () => pm.response.to.have.status(401));
